easy.question: Who heard and reacted at the start of the passage?
answers: Jabin king of Hazor
Joshua
Jobab king of Madon
easy.explanation: The verse begins 'when Jabin king of Hazor had heard' — Jabin is the one who heard.

easy.question: Whom did the king of Hazor send to recruit help (v.1)?
answers: He did not send help
To Jobab king of Madon, to the king of Shimron and to the king of Achshaph
To Joshua and other Israelite leaders
easy.explanation: The verse lists messengers sent to Jobab king of Madon, the king of Shimron and the king of Achshaph.

easy.question: How is the number of soldiers described in verse 4?
answers: Few and limited
Moderate
Many, like the sand on the seashore
easy.explanation: The verse says 'much people, even as the sand ... in multitude' — meaning very many.

medium.question: What does the list of 'the north of the mountains, the plains south of Chinneroth, the valley, and the borders of Dor' in verse 2 indicate?
answers: That forces came from varied geographic regions across the land
That all the kings sat on the same single mountain
That the list names towns only
medium.explanation: The list names different types of regions (mountains, plains, valleys, coastal borders), showing the force came from diverse areas.

medium.question: In the phrase 'the plains south of Chinneroth' (v.2), what direction is indicated by 'south'?
answers: North
South
East
medium.explanation: 'South of Chinneroth' clearly indicates the southern direction relative to Chinneroth.

medium.question: Which peoples are named in verse 3 as inhabitants of those regions?
answers: Medes, Persians and Babylonians
Moabites, Ammonites and Benjamites
Canaanite, Amorite, Hittite, Perizzite, Jebusite and Hivite
medium.explanation: Verse 3 lists the Canaanite, Amorite, Hittite, Perizzite, Jebusite and Hivite.

challenge.question: Which element in verse 4 emphasizes that this was a strong, well-equipped military force?
answers: The description 'much people' alone
The mention of 'horses and chariots'
The analogy to the sea alone
challenge.explanation: The phrase 'with horses and chariots very many' indicates advanced war apparatus and an organized military.

challenge.question: The phrase 'under Hermon' (v.3) most often points to which geographic area?
answers: The southern part of the land
The central region
The far north of the land
challenge.explanation: Hermon is a mountain in the north; 'under Hermon' indicates a northern location.

challenge.question: What tactical conclusion follows from the combined description 'much people ... with horses and chariots very many'?
answers: A serious threat requiring significant organization by Israel
A description of a friendly confederation
That the force was fictional and not real
challenge.explanation: A large number of troops plus many horses and chariots presents a grave military threat needing a major response.

questions.question: Which element in verse 4 emphasizes that this was a strong, well-equipped military force?
answers: The description 'much people' alone
The mention of 'horses and chariots'
The analogy to the sea alone
questions.explanation: The phrase 'with horses and chariots very many' indicates advanced war apparatus and an organized military.

questions.question: The phrase 'under Hermon' (v.3) most often points to which geographic area?
answers: The southern part of the land
The central region
The far north of the land

That the force was fictional and not real

paragraphs.title: Assembly at the waters of Merom and the Lord's promise

easy.question: Who assembled and came to the waters of Merom according to the verse?
answers: All those kings
Joshua and the Israelites
The prophets and elders
easy.explanation: The verse begins 'And when all these kings were met together' — those kings assembled and camped to fight Israel.

easy.question: Where did those kings camp to fight Israel?
answers: In the Sinai desert
At the waters of Merom
On the Jordan River
easy.explanation: The verse explicitly says they came and pitched at the waters of Merom to fight.

easy.question: Does the phrase 'when all these kings were met together, they came and pitched' appear in verses 5–6?
answers: Yes
No
It cannot be determined
easy.explanation: Yes — that phrasing is quoted directly from verse 5.

medium.question: Why did the kings camp together before the battle according to the verse?
answers: To organize and fight as one force against Israel
To hold a market and regional conference
To seek water together
medium.explanation: The verse says they camped together 'to fight against Israel' — their purpose was military.

medium.question: In the command to Joshua 'thou shalt hough their horses' (v.6), what does the English word 'hough' mean? (Context: 'thou shalt hough their horses')
answers: Feed and care for them
Disable or hamstring them
Ride them forward
medium.explanation: To 'hough' means to hamstring or disable the horses so they cannot be used; the context shows disabling enemy cavalry.

medium.question: What will be done to the chariots according to the Lord's instruction (v.6)?
answers: They will be taken for Israel's use
They will be burned with fire
They will be given to servants
medium.explanation: The verse states 'and burn their chariots with fire' — an order to destroy the chariots by burning.

challenge.question: When the verse says 'all of them shall be slain before Israel', who are the 'slain' meant in context?
answers: Only the chief kings
The kings and their fighting men — i.e., the warriors
Only the weapons and chariots
challenge.explanation: 'Slain' refers to those killed in battle — the kings and their soldiers, not just equipment.

challenge.question: Where is the site 'waters of Merom' most likely located based on tradition and geography?
answers: In the north, near the Hula Lake/Jordan valley area
In the Negev desert in the south
On the east bank of the Jordan
challenge.explanation: Merom is traditionally associated with northern locations such as the Hula Lake or nearby Jordan valley, a staging area for armies.

challenge.question: In the Lord's promise 'Be not afraid ... for to morrow about this time will I deliver them up all slain before Israel', what does 'to morrow about this time' mean?
answers: A very distant future time
Soon — the near future (around the next day or shortly)
A purely figurative phrase with no time reference
challenge.explanation: 'To morrow about this time' indicates a near future time — the promise is imminent, not distant or purely figurative.

questions.question: When the verse says 'all of them shall be slain before Israel', who are the 'slain' meant in context?
answers: Only the chief kings
The kings and their fighting men — i.e., the warriors
Only the weapons and chariots
questions.explanation: 'Slain' refers to those killed in battle — the kings and their soldiers, not just equipment.

questions.question: Where is the site 'waters of Merom' most likely located based on tradition and geography?
answers: In the north, near the Hula Lake/Jordan valley area
In the Negev desert in the south
On the east bank of the Jordan
questions.explanation: Merom is traditionally associated with northern locations such as the Hula Lake or nearby Jordan valley, a staging area for armies.

answers: A very distant future time

A purely figurative phrase with no time reference
questions.explanation: 'To morrow about this time' indicates a near future time — the promise is imminent, not distant or purely figurative.

easy.question: Who came upon their enemies suddenly in verse 7?
answers: Joshua alone
Joshua and all the people of war with him
Only the mounted troops
easy.explanation: The verse says 'So Joshua came, and all the people of war with him' — Joshua arrived with his army.

easy.question: What happened at the waters of Merom in verse 7?
answers: They fell upon them
They drank from the waters
They built shelter there
easy.explanation: Verse 7 records that 'they fell upon them' — the enemy was attacked and fell there.

easy.question: After Israel captured the enemy in verse 8, what did they do?
answers: Returned land to them
Made a peace treaty
Struck and pursued them to various cities
easy.explanation: The verse describes striking and pursuing them 'unto great Zidon, and unto Misrephothmaim ...' — a wide pursuit after victory.

medium.question: In the command 'thou shalt hough their horses' (v.6–7 context), what does 'hough' mean? (Context: 'thou shalt hough their horses')
answers: Provide them food and grooming
Disable their ability to run/use (hamstring)
Train them for riding
medium.explanation: To 'hough' means to hamstring or disable the horses; in context this neutralizes the enemy's cavalry.

medium.question: What was done to the enemy chariots in verse 9?
answers: Taken for Israel's use
Burned with fire
Given to slaves
medium.explanation: Verse 9 states 'and he burnt their chariots with fire' — the chariots were destroyed by burning.

medium.question: What does the phrase 'until they left them none remaining' (v.8) mean about the enemy forces?
answers: They left some survivors
They left a single remnant
They left no survivors at all
medium.explanation: The phrase indicates that nothing was left — no survivors remained; the force was eliminated.

challenge.question: What does the word 'suddenly' in verse 7 suggest about the battle plan?
answers: The attack was a surprise with little forewarning
There was a sudden change in weather
The battle lasted many years
challenge.explanation: 'Suddenly' indicates the assault was unexpected and achieved surprise, not a long preparation.

challenge.question: To where did Israel pursue the enemy in verse 8 and what does that indicate about the scope of the fight?
answers: They pursued only near the camp — a small-scale fight
To great Zidon, Misrephothmaim and the valley of Mizpeh eastward — showing a broad northern and eastern pursuit
They pursued briefly and then returned — a small skirmish
challenge.explanation: The verse names distant locations such as Zidon and Misrephothmaim, indicating a wide-ranging pursuit across northern areas.

challenge.question: Why is it sensible that Joshua would 'hough their horses' but 'burn their chariots'?
answers: To prevent the enemy from using horses and chariots later — disabling horses and destroying chariots removes their war capability
Because the horses were sacred and could not be killed
Because they knew how to burn chariots but not repair horses
challenge.explanation: Disabling horses and burning chariots removes the enemy's future military mobility — a deliberate strategy to neutralize their war resources.

questions.question: What does the word 'suddenly' in verse 7 suggest about the battle plan?
answers: The attack was a surprise with little forewarning
There was a sudden change in weather
The battle lasted many years
questions.explanation: 'Suddenly' indicates the assault was unexpected and achieved surprise, not a long preparation.

questions.question: To where did Israel pursue the enemy in verse 8 and what does that indicate about the scope of the fight?
answers: They pursued only near the camp — a small-scale fight
To great Zidon, Misrephothmaim and the valley of Mizpeh eastward — showing a broad northern and eastern pursuit
They pursued briefly and then returned — a small skirmish
questions.explanation: The verse names distant locations such as Zidon and Misrephothmaim, indicating a wide-ranging pursuit across northern areas.

questions.explanation: Disabling horses and burning chariots removes the enemy's future military mobility — a deliberate strategy to neutralize their war resources.

easy.question: Which city did Joshua capture in verse 10?
answers: Acco
Hazor
Jericho
easy.explanation: Verse 10 begins 'And Joshua ... took Hazor' — Hazor is the city captured.

easy.question: What did Joshua do to Hazor according to verse 11?
answers: Burned it with fire
Signed a peace treaty
Rebuilt it
easy.explanation: The verse says 'and he burnt Hazor with fire' — Hazor was burned.

easy.question: According to verse 12, whose command did Joshua follow in this action?
answers: The Lord directly
Aaron
Moses
easy.explanation: Verse 12 states 'as Moses the servant of the Lord commanded' — the instruction is traced to Moses.

medium.question: What happened to 'all the souls that were therein' in verse 11?
answers: They were struck with the edge of the sword and utterly destroyed
They were taken captive and taxed
They were left in peace under Israel's rule
medium.explanation: The verse states all souls were struck with the sword and 'there was not any left to breathe' — they were killed.

medium.question: In the phrase from the verse 'utterly destroying them' (context: 'they utterly destroyed them'), what does that imply?
answers: Dedicating them to complete destruction / annihilation
Subjecting them to a legal trial
Protecting and preserving them
medium.explanation: 'Utterly destroying' in the biblical context means complete destruction or annihilation, not preservation or trial.

medium.question: Which cities were not burned according to verse 13?
answers: Cities that stood on mounds (hill-towns)
All the cities in the region
Only Hazor was not burned
medium.explanation: Verse 13 says 'save cities that stood on mounds were not burned' — hill-towns were exceptions.

challenge.question: What is unusual about Hazor compared to the other cities that stood on mounds?
answers: Hazor was not burned even though mound-cities were burned
Hazor alone was burned even though mound-cities were generally not burned
Hazor was handed over as captives instead of being burned
challenge.explanation: The text explains that only mound-cities were spared, 'save Hazor only' — Hazor was the exception and was burned.

challenge.question: Where is Hazor placed historically in the biblical record?
answers: In the north near the Sea of Galilee/Hula region
West of Jericho in the desert
In the southern Judean hills
challenge.explanation: Hazor is located in the northern Canaan region near the Sea of Galilee and the Hula valley in biblical and archaeological sources.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'there was not any left to breathe' (v.11) mean about the inhabitants?
answers: They were exiled
Many were killed but there were survivors
No person was left alive — all were killed
challenge.explanation: The expression means that no human life remained; everyone was killed, as the verse indicates.

questions.question: What is unusual about Hazor compared to the other cities that stood on mounds?
answers: Hazor was not burned even though mound-cities were burned
Hazor alone was burned even though mound-cities were generally not burned
Hazor was handed over as captives instead of being burned
questions.explanation: The text explains that only mound-cities were spared, 'save Hazor only' — Hazor was the exception and was burned.

questions.question: Where is Hazor placed historically in the biblical record?
answers: In the north near the Sea of Galilee/Hula region
West of Jericho in the desert
In the southern Judean hills
questions.explanation: Hazor is located in the northern Canaan region near the Sea of Galilee and the Hula valley in biblical and archaeological sources.

answers: They were exiled

No person was left alive — all were killed
questions.explanation: The expression means that no human life remained; everyone was killed, as the verse indicates.

paragraphs.title: Plunder, spoil and destruction of the people

easy.question: What did the Israelites take from the cities according to verse 14?
answers: Only the people and settled them
All the spoil of the cities and the cattle
The cities' archives and offices
easy.explanation: The verse says 'all the spoil of these cities, and the cattle' — they took both the spoil and the animals.

easy.question: What did Israel do to every person in those cities in verse 14?
answers: Struck them with the sword until destroyed
Took them captive and spared their lives
Enslaved them and let them live in their villages
easy.explanation: The verse states they struck every person with the sword till destroyed — they killed them.

easy.question: Who gave the command that Joshua followed, according to verse 15?
answers: The Lord directly (without mediation)
The priests in the temple
Moses commanded Joshua in accordance with the Lord's command to Moses
easy.explanation: Verse 15 notes Moses commanded Joshua, as the Lord commanded Moses — the order came via Moses.

medium.question: What is the relationship between the Lord's command to Moses and Joshua's actions in verse 15?
answers: Joshua acted exactly as the Lord commanded through Moses
Joshua refused to follow the command
The verse claims Moses' commands did not reach Joshua
medium.explanation: The verse states Joshua did as Moses (who had Moses' commission from the Lord) commanded — Joshua followed the Lord's instruction via Moses.

medium.question: In the phrase 'all the spoil of these cities' (v.14), what does 'spoil' mean? (Context: 'all the spoil of these cities')
answers: Gifts presented to the victors
Booty or loot taken in war
Legal records and archives
medium.explanation: 'Spoil' means the goods taken as booty or plunder from captured cities; the context lists cattle and spoil taken as prey.

medium.question: What does 'they left none to breathe' in verse 14 imply about the fate of the inhabitants?
answers: They kept some as slaves
They were all destroyed with none left alive
Many were deported
medium.explanation: The phrase clarifies that they left no survivors — the people were completely destroyed.

challenge.question: What can be concluded about the nature of the warfare described in these verses?
answers: It restricted itself to military defeats and did not affect civilians
It preferred negotiation and diplomatic settlement
It was total war: population annihilation and taking of spoil formed part of the victory
challenge.explanation: The passages speak of complete destruction ('left none to breathe') and taking of spoil and cattle — indicating comprehensive warfare including annihilation and plunder.

challenge.question: What biblical term fits the idea of devotion to destruction and prohibition on taking certain spoils (as seen here)?
answers: Herem
Covenant
Judgement
challenge.explanation: The concept 'herem' in the Bible denotes devotion to destruction or prohibition — often used in the context of commanded destruction in holy war.

challenge.question: What does the phrase 'he left nothing undone of all that the Lord commanded Moses' (v.15) indicate about Joshua's conduct?
answers: He tended to change or adapt the commands to his preference
He faithfully carried out all the commands without omitting anything
He refused to carry out most commands and acted on his own judgment
challenge.explanation: 'Left nothing undone' means Joshua did not omit or alter the commands — he executed them fully and faithfully.

questions.question: What can be concluded about the nature of the warfare described in these verses?
answers: It restricted itself to military defeats and did not affect civilians

It was total war: population annihilation and taking of spoil formed part of the victory

answers: Herem
Covenant
Judgement
questions.explanation: The concept 'herem' in the Bible denotes devotion to destruction or prohibition — often used in the context of commanded destruction in holy war.

answers: He tended to change or adapt the commands to his preference
He faithfully carried out all the commands without omitting anything
He refused to carry out most commands and acted on his own judgment
questions.explanation: 'Left nothing undone' means Joshua did not omit or alter the commands — he executed them fully and faithfully.

easy.question: Who took the land described in verse 16?
answers: Moses
Joshua
David
easy.explanation: The verse opens 'So Joshua took all that land' — Joshua is the one who took it.

easy.question: Which place name does NOT appear in the list of areas in verse 16?
answers: The hills and the south country
The land of Goshen
Baal-gad
easy.explanation: Verse 16 lists hills, south country, land of Goshen, valley, plain and mountain of Israel; Baal-gad is mentioned in verse 17.

easy.question: What did Joshua do to their kings in verse 17?
answers: Captured, struck and slew them
Made a treaty with them
Relocated them elsewhere
easy.explanation: Verse 17 states he took all their kings, smote them and slew them — he captured and killed them.

medium.question: In the phrase 'the hills, and all the south country' (v.16), what does 'the south country' refer to?
answers: A desert area in the far south
The southern portion of the land
A coastal plain only
medium.explanation: 'South country' denotes the southern region of the land — the southern part of the territory taken.

medium.question: What is the northern limit of the conquest as given in verse 17?
answers: Mount Halak up to Seir and Baal-gad in the valley of Lebanon under Hermon
Seir in the far south
The Negev in the south
medium.explanation: Verse 17 names 'from mount Halak ... even unto Baal-gad in the valley of Lebanon under mount Hermon' — a northern boundary near Hermon.

medium.question: How do verses 16 and 17 relate to each other?
answers: 16 talks about construction; 17 about agriculture
16 records the general taking of the land; 17 specifies the limits and the kings taken
16 reports a retreat; 17 reports peaceful settlement
medium.explanation: Verse 16 gives a summary of the territory taken, while verse 17 details the geographical limits and the kings Joshua captured.

challenge.question: What small detail might be easy to miss in the list of places in verse 16?
answers: The verse mentions only mountainous regions
It lists both lowlands (the plain) and the south country (the Arabah) as well
It mentions only north and south but no low areas
challenge.explanation: The verse mentions a variety of landscape types — hills, the south country, the valley and the plain — showing control over diverse terrain.

challenge.question: What does the sequence 'he took, and smote them, and slew them' (v.17) convey?
answers: They negotiated and surrendered peacefully
A sequence of decisive military actions: capture, defeat and killing
The kings were conscripted into Joshua's army
challenge.explanation: The trio of verbs shows a series of forceful actions culminating in decisive military defeat and death.

challenge.question: How does the phrase 'in the valley of Lebanon under mount Hermon' help locate the conquest boundary?
answers: It points to a northern spot near Mount Hermon — the northern limit of Joshua's conquest
It indicates a southern area in the Judean desert
It describes an island in the Mediterranean
challenge.explanation: The phrase identifies a northern area near Hermon, clarifying that Joshua's control extended to the northern frontier.

questions.question: What small detail might be easy to miss in the list of places in verse 16?
answers: The verse mentions only mountainous regions
It lists both lowlands (the plain) and the south country (the Arabah) as well
It mentions only north and south but no low areas
questions.explanation: The verse mentions a variety of landscape types — hills, the south country, the valley and the plain — showing control over diverse terrain.

questions.question: What does the sequence 'he took, and smote them, and slew them' (v.17) convey?
answers: They negotiated and surrendered peacefully
A sequence of decisive military actions: capture, defeat and killing
The kings were conscripted into Joshua's army
questions.explanation: The trio of verbs shows a series of forceful actions culminating in decisive military defeat and death.

answers: It points to a northern spot near Mount Hermon — the northern limit of Joshua's conquest
It indicates a southern area in the Judean desert
It describes an island in the Mediterranean
questions.explanation: The phrase identifies a northern area near Hermon, clarifying that Joshua's control extended to the northern frontier.

paragraphs.title: Long wars and the exception of Gibeon

easy.question: Who made all these wars according to the verse?
answers: Joshua
Moses
A later king
easy.explanation: The verse begins 'And Joshua made war a long time with all those kings' — Joshua conducted the wars.

easy.question: Was there any city that made peace with Israel according to the verse?
answers: No, no city made peace
Yes — the Hivites, inhabitants of Gibeon
Yes — every city made peace
easy.explanation: The verse says no city made terms with Israel except the Hivites who lived in Gibeon — Gibeon is the exception.

easy.question: What happened to the other cities according to the verse?
answers: They were preserved and taxed
They were taken by war
They were left untouched
easy.explanation: The verse concludes 'all other they took in battle' — the remaining cities were captured by force.

medium.question: What does the verse imply about the fate of most Canaanite cities?
answers: They made peace with Israel
Most were taken and conquered in battle
They remained independent
medium.explanation: The phrase 'all other they took in battle' indicates the majority of cities were conquered militarily.

medium.question: In the phrase 'made peace with the children of Israel' (v.19), what does 'made peace' mean in context?
answers: Surrendered by force
Entered into a treaty or terms of peace
Completed a public work
medium.explanation: Here 'made peace' denotes reaching terms or a treaty with Israel rather than forced submission or unrelated activity.

medium.question: What does the expression 'a long time' at the start of verse 18 suggest?
answers: Short, brief engagements
A prolonged period of military campaigns
A precise count of many centuries
medium.explanation: 'A long time' indicates sustained, extended military activity — a prolonged campaign rather than a single short battle.

challenge.question: Given other biblical passages (e.g., chapter 9), what can be inferred about Israel's relationship with Gibeon?
answers: Gibeon was destroyed and left in ruins
Gibeon made peace with Israel and remained, entering a covenant/arrangement
Gibeon vanished without trace
challenge.explanation: Chapter 9 describes Gibeon's treaty with Israel; here Gibeon is the exceptional city that made peace and therefore remained.

challenge.question: What is the role of the word 'save' (as in 'save the Hivites') in the verse 'There was not a city ... save the Hivites the inhabitants of Gibeon'?
answers: Adds emphasis to the word 'city'
Indicates future time
Marks an exception — 'except' or 'besides'
challenge.explanation: 'Save' here functions like 'except', highlighting Gibeon as the exception to the general rule.

challenge.question: Who were the 'Hivites inhabitants of Gibeon' in the historical-biblical sense?
answers: Local Canaanite people (the Hivites) living in Gibeon
A family within the tribe of Judah
A group of nomadic merchants from abroad
challenge.explanation: The Hivites were one of the Canaanite peoples; the phrase refers to the local Hivite population dwelling in Gibeon.

questions.question: Given other biblical passages (e.g., chapter 9), what can be inferred about Israel's relationship with Gibeon?
answers: Gibeon was destroyed and left in ruins
Gibeon made peace with Israel and remained, entering a covenant/arrangement
Gibeon vanished without trace
questions.explanation: Chapter 9 describes Gibeon's treaty with Israel; here Gibeon is the exceptional city that made peace and therefore remained.

questions.question: What is the role of the word 'save' (as in 'save the Hivites') in the verse 'There was not a city ... save the Hivites the inhabitants of Gibeon'?
answers: Adds emphasis to the word 'city'
Indicates future time
Marks an exception — 'except' or 'besides'
questions.explanation: 'Save' here functions like 'except', highlighting Gibeon as the exception to the general rule.

questions.question: Who were the 'Hivites inhabitants of Gibeon' in the historical-biblical sense?
answers: Local Canaanite people (the Hivites) living in Gibeon
A family within the tribe of Judah
A group of nomadic merchants from abroad
questions.explanation: The Hivites were one of the Canaanite peoples; the phrase refers to the local Hivite population dwelling in Gibeon.

paragraphs.title: The Lord hardens and the extermination of the Anakim

easy.question: Why did the Lord harden the hearts of the Canaanite kings (v.20)?
answers: So they would stand and fight Israel
So they would flee from Israel's presence
So they would consult together
easy.explanation: The verse says the Lord hardened their hearts so they would come to battle against Israel.

easy.question: Who did Joshua cut off from the mountains (v.21)?
answers: The Philistines
The Anakim (the giants)
The priests
easy.explanation: The text says Joshua cut off the Anakims from the mountains — referring to those giant clans.

easy.question: In which cities did remnants of the Anakim remain according to verse 22?
answers: Hebron, Debir, Anab
All cities of Judah
Gaza, Gath and Ashdod
easy.explanation: Verse 22 lists Gaza, Gath and Ashdod as the places where Anakim remained.

medium.question: How does verse 20 present the reason the Canaanite kings attacked Israel?
answers: The Lord strengthened their hearts so they would come against Israel in battle
They wished to conquer Israel out of fear
They were invited to sign a treaty with Joshua
medium.explanation: The verse attributes the initiative to God's hardening of their hearts, causing them to engage Israel in battle.

medium.question: In the phrase 'Joshua destroyed them utterly' (v.21 context), what does 'destroyed them utterly' indicate?
answers: Devoted them to complete destruction (annihilation)
Recorded their names in a list
Enlisted them into Israel's service
medium.explanation: 'Destroyed them utterly' conveys total annihilation or complete removal, not registration or assimilation.

medium.question: Which locations are mentioned as sources from which Joshua removed the Anakim (v.21)?
answers: Gaza, Gath, Ashdod
From the mountain, from Hebron, Debir and Anab and all the mountains of Judah
The Sea of Galilee and the valleys
medium.explanation: Verse 21 specifies Hebron, Debir, Anab and the mountains of Judah and Israel as places Joshua cut off the Anakim.

challenge.question: What can be inferred about the condition of the Anakim after Joshua's actions?
answers: They disappeared from the mountainous regions and only remained in the Philistine coastal cities
They made peace with Israel and integrated
